description: Test your knowledge of PA H1 | Hematopoiesis & Blood Specimen Basics.

cards.text: What is haematopoiesis, and where does it occur?
cards.answer: Haematopoiesis is the continuous process of blood cell production from haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in the bone marrow. The term comes from Greek: haima (blood) + poiēsis (making).

tip.tip: Think 'making blood' — that's literally what haematopoiesis means.

cards.text: What are the two defining properties of a haematopoietic stem cell (HSC)?
cards.answer: Self-renewal: ability to divide and produce daughter HSCs to maintain the pool for life. Multipotency: ability to commit to any blood cell lineage. HSCs comprise only 0.01% of bone marrow cells.

tip.tip: HSCs have two superpowers: self-renew AND go anywhere (multipotent).

cards.text: What two progenitor families arise from the HSC, and what lineages does each produce?
cards.answer: CMP (common myeloid progenitor) produces RBCs, platelets, neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. CLP (common lymphoid progenitor) produces T-cells, B-cells, and NK cells.

tip.tip: CMP = all non-lymphoid cells; CLP = lymphoid cells only.

cards.text: Name the four key growth factors in haematopoiesis and their primary targets.
cards.answer: EPO (kidney → erythropoiesis; rises in hypoxia), TPO (liver/kidney → megakaryopoiesis/platelets), G-CSF (→ neutrophil production and HSC mobilisation), SCF (→ HSC survival and proliferation).

cards.text: At which erythroid maturation stage is the nucleus extruded, and what happens to it?
cards.answer: At the orthochromatic erythroblast stage, the nucleus is extruded (ejected from the cell) and immediately phagocytosed by bone marrow macrophages. This is why mature RBCs have no nucleus.

tip.tip: Ortho = last nucleated stage; nucleus gets kicked out and eaten by macrophages.

cards.text: At which stage of erythroid maturation does haemoglobin synthesis begin, and what morphological change indicates it?
cards.answer: Haemoglobin synthesis begins at the polychromatic erythroblast stage. The cytoplasm changes colour from dark blue (RNA-rich) to blue-pink as haemoglobin accumulates.

tip.tip: Polychromatic = 'many colours' = blue-pink = Hb coming in.

cards.text: What does reticulocyte count tell you about bone marrow function in anaemia?
cards.answer: High reticulocyte count indicates an effective marrow response (e.g., compensation for bleeding or haemolysis). Low reticulocyte count in anaemia suggests marrow failure (aplasia, EPO deficiency, or inability to respond).

tip.tip: Retics rising = marrow working hard; retics low in anaemia = marrow trouble.

cards.text: How long does erythropoiesis take from EPO stimulus to mature RBC release into circulation?
cards.answer: Approximately 7 days from EPO stimulus to release of mature erythrocytes into the peripheral blood.

tip.tip: Seven days from stimulus to mature RBC — a useful timeline for clinical reasoning in anaemia.
